title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - Fine against HAYAT MEDICAL & DENTAL S.R.L
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
As part of its dental care activities, Hayat Medical & Dental SRL (the controller) processed patients’ names and phone numbers, which were subsequently accessed and disclosed. Following a complaint lodged by a data subject, the Romanian DPA launched an investigation, during which the controller failed to provide all the information requested by the authority.


Holding[edit | edit source]
Regarding the controller’s cooperation with the DPA, ANSPDCP held that it failed to provide all the information requested in the exercise of its investigative powers, in breach of Article 58(1)(a) GDPR and Article 58(1)€ GDPR, in conjunction with Article 83 GDPR(5)(e).
Regarding the processing of patients’ personal data, ANSPDCP found that the controller processed the data without a legal basis, including by accessing and disclosing patients’ names and phone numbers. The DPA therefore found a violation of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6(1) GDPR.
In this context, the DPA decided to fine the controller €2,000 (RON 10,700) for failing to provide the requested information and €3,000 (RON 16,050) for unlawfully processing patients’ personal data.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - Auchan Romania S.A
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Auchan Romania S.A. (controller), a retailer, gave unauthorised access of the personal data of a significant number of data subjects (internal users) to a third party following a cyberattack on an administrator account of one of the operator’s security systems. The personal data disclosed included the usernames, first names, last names, email addresses and passwords of the data subjects. 
The controller notified the DPA about the security breach and the DPA launched an investigation. During the investigation, the DPA found that at the time of the cyberattack, the controller had not implemented sufficient security measures concerning secure access to their network storage device. The implementation of sufficient measures would have mitigated the risk of the cyberattack.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the controller has failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to ensure the confidentiality of their processing system and services. This failure led to the cyberattack. The DPA found a violation of Article 32(1)(b) GDPR and Article 32(2) GDPR.
The DPA issued a fine of RON 41,908 (€8,000). Pursuant to Article 58(2)(d) GDPR, the DPA ordered the controller to carry out the technical and organizational implementation of access rules for all of the controller’s IT equipment exclusively from the company’s internal network. In cases where external access is deemed necessary, the DPA ordered the controller to access their system at least through the simultaneous use of a VPN and multi-factor authentication.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00114/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A data subject sent a complaint to Giants Gaming Esports S.L. (the controller) alerting them of a data breach. The complaint concerned a data breach involving the sensitive and personal data of 80,581 data subjects. The data was part of a filing system which could be downloaded through a URL, and included first and last names, account IDs, city, province, post code and gender of users. 
The controller notified the DPA of the data breach, and the DPA initiated an investigation. 
Upon its investigation, the DPA established that whilst the data subject reported the data breach, the controller did not contact the enterprise managing its databases until a month later. The controller claimed that the incident was a result of a configuration error which exposed the filing system containing the controller’s user’s personal data. The controller emphasised that despite the breach, the information was not made visible on search engines, social media or other websites.
Additionally, the DPA understood that the controller, upon receiving notification, did not take necessary measures to verify that the personal data of its customers and users was exposed. Furthermore, the controller had received an email from the managing enterprise that the creation of this filing system containing sensitive information went beyond practices undertaken by a system administrator.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that whilst it is true that the exposure of the filing system did not make the information available on websites, search engines and on social media. The DPA took into account the fact that the data was visible and accessible via the internet for almost a month. This ultimately affected the confidentiality of 80,581 data subjects’ personal data.
This in connection with the fact that someone created this filing system, which was an unusual practice, was a clear indication for the DPA that the controller lacked the necessary technical and organisational measures to mitigate against a data breach risk.
As a result, the DPA held that the controller was in violation of Article 32 GDPR. The fine was initially set at €6,000 but pursuant to Law 39/2015, a Spanish law concerning administrative proceedings, the DPA informed the controller that it may make a voluntary payment of the proposed fine and waive their right to appeal. This action reduces the imposed fine by 20%. The controller opted to make a voluntary payment and reduced the fine by 20%, paying the reduced sanction amount of €4,800.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 747/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint by an employee of Poste Italiane S.p.A. (the data subject) after Deutsche Bank denied the data subjects loan application, and subsequently published on its platform that the data subject had outstanding payments, specified the amount and their net income. Importantly, this platform was accessible to all Poste Italiane S.p.A.’s staff which is responsible for loan application management, and the staff of the Portacomaro Stazione Post Office of the Municipality of Asti. 
The data subject expressed that submitting the form was necessary for a loan application, however did not include a field to enter their salary. This information was to be provided directly by Poste Italiane S.p.A., and that Deutsche Bank would only disclose the outcome of the verification to Poste Italiane S.p.A. which would then communicate it to the data subject. The data subject objected to the processing of their data and requested the erasure of such data from Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. granted the data subject their request, however the data subject deemed the responses unsatisfactory. 
The DPA launched a preliminary investigation into the Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. (the data subject chose not to file a complaint against the latter) requesting clarification of the contractual relationship, respective roles in terms of data protection and privacy, and the data processing practices related to loan applications and the data exchanged between the two.
In its response, Poste Italiane S.p.A. clarified that the relationship with Deutsche Bank was governed by an agreement regarding a loan which could be extended to customers of Poste Italiane S.p.A. under certain conditions. Furthermore, for privacy purposes, in line with the aforementioned agreement the two of them act as independent controllers. Nonetheless, Deutsche Bank emphasised that it also acts as a processor for Poste Italiane S.p.A. concerning the data communicated to the latter regarding the evaluation criteria for a loan applicant. Conversely, Poste Italiane S.p.A. acts as a processor for Deutsche Bank as regards the data exchange concerning the outcome of the preliminary review of a loan application.
Poste Italiane S.p.A. further emphasised its role in managing loan requests through their independent IT system which is integrated with that of Deutsche Bank for the aforementioned data exchanges. 
Finally, Poste Italiane S.p.A. stated that without delay upon having received the data subject’s requests, they deleted the data and made sure that all staff with access to such data were authorised to do so and trained in data protection.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that Deutsche Bank on the one hand independently determines the processing purposes and essential means related to the data subject’s creditworthiness analysis and has the sole authority to grant or deny the loan. Whereas on the other hand, Poste Italiane S.p.A. operates on a separate contractual relationship with the data subject and processes personal data for its own purposes. Ultimately, it was made evident to the DPA that the processing activities including the disclosure by Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. fell within the scope of what is necessary for the performance of their respective contractual obligations or precontractual measures requested by the data subject (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR). 
Therefore, the DPA held that the decision to designate each other (Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A.) as processors under Article 28 GDPR was contrary to the Article 4(8) GDPR, which defines a processor as the entity processing on behalf and under the instructions of a controller. Namely because the DPA held that the factual assessment of the relationship demonstrates that the disclosure of information between them is carried out by each of them for their own purposes. Ultimately, according to the DPA this makes them independent controllers. 
The DPA found that this wrong designation as processors had direct implications on the compliance with Article 13 GDPR particularly in regards to the privacy notice. Furthermore, The DPA found that Poste Italiane S.p.A.’s privacy notice had not been properly worded and over simplified. This amounted to a violation of Article 13(1)(a) GDPR and Article 5(1)(a) GDPR as the privacy notice was not sufficiently clear and transparent for data subjects. 
As a result of the aforementioned, the DPA found Poste Italiane S.p.A. in violation of the principles of fairness and transparency under Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, lacked the necessary information in its privacy notice in accordance with Article 13(1)(a) GDPR, and wrongly designated each other as processors under Article 28 GDPR. Accordingly, the DPA fined Poste Italiane S.p.A. €48,000.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00372/2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint by a data subject, concerning the Canary Islands Foundation for the Promotion of Special Adapted Transportation’s (the controller) established a biometric time-recording system for its employees in order to track its employees’ working hours. The system functioned through time-stamping using the fingerprints of its employees.
Such biometric data processing of employees’ fingerprints was undertaken from October 2023 until March 2024 and split into two phases. The first phase consisted of mandatory biometric data processing through this system and the second phase only included the processing of employee’s biometric data who consented.
During the proceedings, the controller did not present any evidence which demonstrated that one of the Article 9(2) GDPR exceptions were applicable and thus allowing for such processing. The controller submitted two data protection impact assessments (DPIA), one of which did not entail a date or signature by the controller. The second DPIA was a generic assessment that the processor conducted for all the time-and-attendance systems managed by it. It included both biometric and non-biometric systems and covered the specific case of fingerprint processing.


Holding[edit | edit source]
Regarding the necessity for an exception to the prohibition of processing special category data under Article 9(1) GDPR, the DPA dismissed the violation. Particularly, because the controller replaced the system with a new card-based system.
The DPA held that the controller did not undertake the necessary three-part assessment of suitability, necessity and strict proportionality of implementing such a system. In determining the necessity of the system, the controller did not assess whether there were less intrusive alternatives and neither did it weigh the benefits of the system against the potential harm to data subjects. 
Furthermore, in light of the category of data being processed (biometric fingerprint data) the DPA stressed the necessity for conducting a proper risk assessment and subsequently implementing measures which mitigate against the established risks posed by the system.
The DPA found that the controller implemented measures for established risks in a very vague, generic and abstract manner. The DPA further held that the controller lacked implementing security measures to prevent breaches or human error. Evidently, the DPA found that the measures provided by the controller were not specifically tailored to the circumstances and characteristics of the system.
Therefore, the DPA held that whilst an impact assessment was conducted and deemed the system to be acceptable as regards the risks posed, it did not meet the requirements for necessity, suitability, and proportionality as required by the GDPR. Neither did the controller conduct a proper risk assessment and correspondingly implement the necessary measures to mitigate against the risks posed by the system.
In light of the foregoing, the DPA found that the controller violated its obligations under Article 35 GDPR as it did not conduct a sufficient enough DPIA for biometric data processing through its system. The DPA held it was sufficient to simply declare the controller’s infringement and thus did not impose a fine.

title: BVwG - W256 2280818-2
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
On 5 January 2022, a professional photographer and video producer (the controller) sent an unsolicited business-to-business (B2B) marketing newsletter via email to the managing director of a company (the data subject). To send the email, the controller used Mailchimp, a US-based email marketing platform operated by The Rocket Science Group, LLC (the processor). Consequently, the data subject's publicly accessible business contact details—specifically his first and last name, company name, and email address—were transferred to the US


Holding[edit | edit source]
Ruling directly on the merits pursuant to Section 28(7) VwGVG following the DSB’s failure to decide, the Federal Administrative Court (BVwG) upheld the data subject’s complaint and declared that the controller violated Articles 44 et seq. GDPR by transferring the data subject’s personal data (name, company name, and email address) to the processor in the US on January 5, 2022. No adequacy decision under Article 45(3) GDPR applied, as the EU-US Privacy Shield had been invalidated in Schrems II (C-311/18) and the 2023 EU-US Data Privacy Framework was adopted after the transfer occurred. Because the processor had not yet implemented the 2021 SCCs, the transfer relied on the 2010 SCCs (Decision 2010/87/EU) and supplementary safeguards under Article 46(1) and (2)(c) GDPR. However, the BVwG found these insufficient: as an "electronic communications service" provider under US law, the processor was subject to mandatory intelligence disclosure orders under Section 702 FISA and Executive Order 12333—which its transparency reports confirmed actually occurred—and contractual clauses could not bind third-country authorities.
Furthermore, the BVwG held that the controller’s supplementary measures failed to close the legal protection gaps identified in Schrems II. Transparency reports, internal directives, and staff training could not override mandatory US disclosure laws, and encryption only protected against unauthorized third parties because the processor remained legally obligated to disclose imported data in its possession or control—including the cryptographic keys—to US authorities (EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, para. 81). Notification and suspension clauses were equally ineffective, as intelligence agencies could prohibit notifying the controller, the controller lacked any effective legal remedy against a US agency, and suspending transfers could not protect already transferred data. Applying the accountability principle (Article 5(2) and 5(1)(a) GDPR) and finding no Article 49 GDPR derogation, the BVwG rejected the controller’s "risk-based" defense: neither Schrems II, Article 44 GDPR ("any" transfer), nor the EDPB distinguished based on the low sensitivity of public B2B data or the low likelihood of government access. Finally, the BVwG excluded the data subject’s June 2025 claims regarding IP addresses, tracking pixels, and profiling as outside the scope of the default complaint (Säumnisbeschwerde, Section 8 VwGVG), dispensed with an oral hearing (Section 24(4) VwGVG), and declared an appeal (Revision) inadmissible (Article 133(4) B-VG).

title: Rb. Noord-Holland - C/15/373813
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
On 14 October 2025, a data subject requested Geestelijke Gezondheidszorg, the Dutch sector association for mental health and addiction services (controller), to remove or correct personal data from its systems. The data subject was or has been client during this request, and is of the opinion that the data are factually incorrect and are not based on police or judicial information since he had not committed any criminal offences. Therefore, he submitted different statements as a matter of the request, and brought this case to court.
According to the controller, they are legally obliged to keep a medical file, which is based on information provided by third parties. This information was used in a court hearing on 7 March 2022 for an authorisation of a crisis measure, while following the procedures of the Compulsory Mental Healthcare Act (Wvggz).[1] This law has a retention period of five years after the end of the crisis measure. Since the measure ran against the data subject until 18 October 2024, a request of deletion cannot in principle be made before 18 October 2029. Therefore, the controller did not comply with this request.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Court held that Article 16 GDPR is only intended to correct inaccuracies that can be easily and objectively verified, thus not professional impressions, opinions, research results or conclusions. The statements provided by the data subject qualified as professional conclusions, which do not fall under the right on rectification under Article 16 GDPR. It makes no difference whether there has been no conviction, since this does not follow declarations that have been made by professionals. Therefore, the court rejects the request to rectify this information.
Additionally, the Court rejects a request to the deletion of personal data based on Article 17 GDPR. First, the data subject did not refer to one of the six grounds in his request. Second, two exceptions are applicable under Article 17(3) GDPR. Deletion of personal data is not possible under Article 17(3)(b) GDPR, since there is a legal obligation in the Dutch Civil Code to keep a medical record. Additionally, there is no right to deletion based on Article 17(3)(d) GDPR, since the personal data had already been used in court to grant the authorisation of the crisis measures.


↑ https://www.dwangindezorg.nl/wvggz/english-version

title: BlnBDI (Berlin) - 521.17130.38
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
An advertisement for the Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU; the controller) was displayed to a Facebook user (the data subject) shortly before the German federal elections in September 2021. At the time, the data subject was using a browser extension which reveals the targeting criteria used to select specific users to display ads to. According to the browser extension, the controller chose to display this specific ad to the data subject based on their age, gender, place of residence, and interest in the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD).
The data subject filed a complaint with the Berlin DPA in March 2023. The controller confirmed that it had commissioned the advertisement displayed to the data subject from Facebook and targeted it to users based on the aforementioned criteria.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA issued the controller a reprimand for infringements of Articles 9(1) and (2), 13(3) and 26(1) and (2) GDPR.
First, the DPA held that the CDU and Meta jointly determined the purposes and means of processing and were acting as joint controllers pursuant to Article 26(1) GDPR with regard to the targeted advertising. The DPA pointed out that Meta offers its customers categories of targeting criteria and collects personal data such as name, place of residence, gender, date of birth, and interests based on their activity its platforms. The advertisers can then select certain targeting criteria in order to decide which users advertisements are displayed to.
There was no transparent arrangement between the joint controllers as required by Article 26 GDPR. Meta's various terms of service and privacy notice lacked specific reference to the CDU as well as clauses determining the controllers’ responsibilities and therefore did not meet the requirements for such an agreement.
Second, the DPA found that the controller had violated Articles 9(1) and (2) GDPR by processing personal data from which the data subject's political opinions could be inferred to target advertising to the data subject without an applicable exception. In the present case, the sensitive personal data consisted of the overall view resulting from the data subject's interactions with content related to the SPD, which led Meta to assume that the data subject belonged to the SPD's voter base.
No explicit consent to process political opinion data had been granted by the data subject. The data could not be considered manifestly made public by the data subject, as not all user interactions used to assign Facebook users to specific interest categories are visible to the public. There was also no substantial public interest in the targeted display of election campaign advertising using political opinion data. On the contrary, the DPA pointed out that microtargeting based on sensitive personal data conflicts with the public interest in fair and uninfluenced elections.
Finally, the DPA held that the controller was subject to the obligations set forth in Article 13(3) GDPR, as it further processed personal data collected by Meta to target advertising to data subjects. The controller had not provided the data subject information on the purpose of processing or the relevant information pursuant to Article 13(2) GDPR prior to the further processing.

title: Datatilsynet (Denmark) - 2025-31-2353
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A data subject submitted an access request to Metro Service A/S (the controller) for access to the CCTV footage from a metro station concerning a specific incident where the data subject was involved. The data subject included a general description of their appearance and information about certain details about the day. The controller refused access to the data subject. The data subject submitted a complaint to the DPA.
The controller refused to grant access on the basis that the incident was not specifically pinpointed (the data subject indicated a 10-day period between 12:00am and 6:00am) and thus was unable to identify the complainant. Additionally, the controller claimed that granting access would have been time-consuming and that in light of public safety certain CCTV footage cannot be disclosed. Finally, the controller stated that providing access could have allowed for the exposure of blind spots. 
After having notified the data subject of the denial of their request, the controller subsequently deleted the CCTV footage. Under normal circumstances, the controller clarified that footage is deleted after 30 days.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller could not have relied on lack of identification, excessive time consumption or public safety. 
Lack of identification and excessive nature of request
Primarily, the DPA found that the controller did not sufficiently demonstrate that the description given by the data subject did not allow for their identification in the footage. The DPA placed emphasis on the fact that the data subject included both a physical description and description of the entire incident, which took place at a time where the station was not so crowded. Combined, it held that the controller violated Articles 12(2) and 15 GDPR as it could have identified the data subject and specific incident referred to in the access request.
Furthermore, the DPA held that in order to be exempt from fulfilling a data subjects access request, the controller bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive. The DPA found that the controller was unable to sufficiently demonstrate why editing the footage would make it impossible to identify the incident and take an excessive amount of time. The DPA emphasised that the controller has a choice to implement such technologies and that this does not exempt from the obligation to ensure that the processing operations enable compliance with data subject rights.
Public Safety
The DPA found that the controller did not sufficiently demonstrate that a balancing of conflicting interests, was conducted which would allow for the exemption from having to grant the access request. Particularly, the DPA held that the controller did not assess the camera’s position and the specific public safety considerations that the camera angle and position may entail against the data subjects’ rights. 
Deletion of footage post access refusal
Additionally, the DPA found that the controller deleting the information about the data subject immediately after refusing their access request was contrary to the principle of lawfulness, transparency and fairness (Article 5(1)(a) GDPR). Particularly, as it unlawfully deprived the data subject of the possibility of having their right of access reviewed by the DPA or by courts to verify whether a data subject is entitled to access the information.
Moreover, the DPA emphasised that for the purposes of fulfilling a specific request to access, the footage covering the 10-day period could have been retained beyond the established deletion deadline.
Finally, the DPA stressed the likeliness of other individuals being captured by the footage, and that the controller should have thus implemented technical measures to ensure that the data subject only receives information about themselves.
In light of its assessment, the DPA issued a reprimand against the controller for refusing to grant access to the data subject and the subsequent deletion of the data. This amounted to violations of Article 5(1)(a), 12(2), 12(5)(b) and 15 GDPR.

title: HDPA (Greece) - 19/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint from a former employee of the Service 800 Teleperformance Single Member S.A. (the controller), after the controller failed to comply with the data subjects access request.
In his request, the data subject wanted to be informed of whether any data concerning him are being processed, access to copies of all electronic messages, and specifics about the controllers processing operations. The data subject also requested the documents containing comments, evaluations, disciplinary measures or written warnings, concerning the past issues of psychological abuse and workplace mistreatment they underwent.
Within a month, the controller responded to the data subject by extended its response period by 60 days without a reason and offering some information of what was requested. The data subject contacted the controller again and requested a full response as well as reasoning for the extension of the response period. The controller never justified the extension period and since, barred the data subject from accessing the workplace without cause.
The controller stated that before the data subject was hired, he was provided with, and signed the controller’s privacy notice, and therefore deemed him well aware of the processing operations, and purpose of such. Furthermore, the controller clarified that on the last day of employment all accounts are deactivated, and access is terminated. Specifying that in accordance with their policies all the data in the email account is permanently deleted within 24 hours, and the company issued laptop is wiped of all locally stored data. As a result, the controller was unable to provide the data subject with the requested emails. Ultimately, the controller claimed that after removing all data pertaining to third parties, they provided the data subject with all his information. Any subsequent failure to provide information was a result of the application of established security and access termination policies.
The DPA found the data subject’s complaint unfounded and dismissed the case. The data subject requested reconsideration believing that the DPA dismissed on the basis of legal and factual errors.
In their appeal, the data subject expressed that the request was submitted before their last day of work (half a month before) which contradicts the claim by the controller that the request was submitted after the deletion. Moreover, the data subject emphasised that the right of access pertains to the time that the request was submitted, and that the deletion policies do not exempt the controller from retaining data until the termination of the employment relationship. Finally, the data subject mentioned that they submitted a request that the emails and data related to the complaints of workplace abuse and mistreatment and related evidence should not be deleted.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller failed to provide the data subject with the information requested and unlawfully proceeded to delete the data before the termination of the employment relationship. Accordingly, the DPA found a violation of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 15 and 17(3)(e) GDPR.
Furthermore, the DPA found that the controller failed to explicitly and clearly justify the extension of response period, violating Article 12(3) GDPR.
The DPA also held that the data retention period was not communicated to the data subject violating Article 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR.
Moreover, the DPA found a violation of Article 32 GDPR as the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the availability to the data subject to their personal data. Similarly, the controller failed to implement an appropriate procedure to prevent the deletion of the data. Instead, the controller applied a blanket deletion policy.
Finally, the DPA found a violation of Article 5(2) GDPR as the controller did not take appropriate measures to handle the request of the data subject lawfully.
As a result of the foregoing violations of the GDPR, the DPA fined the controller €60,000 for the violations of Article 5(1)(a) and (f), 15, and 17(3)(e) GDPR, and €40,000 for violating Articles 5(2), 12(3), 13 and 32 GDPR.

title: BVerwG - 6 C 9.25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A passenger (the data subject) requested the operator of the S-Bahn network in Berlin (the controller) to provide them a copy of the video recordings of a train journey which featured the data subject in October 2020. The controller rejected this request, and the data subject lodged a complaint with the Berlin DPA. In December 2021, the DPA reprimanded the controller for a violation of Article 15 GDPR due to its refusal to provide the data subject with the requested information.
The controller appealed the DPA decision to the Berlin Administrative Court (VG Berlin). The administrative court overturned the contested reprimand. The DPA appealed the decision of the administrative court to the Berlin-Brandenburg Higher Administrative Court (OVG Berlin-Brandenburg). The higher administrative court dismissed the appeal and upheld the administrative court’s decision in May 2025, stating that the controller could refuse to provide the data subject a copy of the requested video recordings. 
Parallel to the administrative proceedings, the data subject had brought civil proceedings seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damages under Article 82 GDPR before the Pankow Local Court (AG Pankow). This lawsuit and the subsequent appeal to the Regional Court were both dismissed as no GDPR violation could be found. 
The data subject filed an appeal before the Federal Administrative Court (Bundesverwaltungsgericht) and requested to be joined in the appeal proceedings concerning the overturned reprimand as an intervenor.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the data subject’s appeal. 
The court pointed out that an appeal by an intervenor is only admissible if the contested decision results in an independent, substantive adverse effect on the intervenor. In addition, the adverse effect must relate to the individual’s legal status. In the present case, the administrative court decision overturning the reprimand did not adversely affect the intervenor’s substantive legal position: a civil court had already found in a judgment with final and binding effect between the same parties that no GDPR violation had occurred. The data subject could therefore no longer assert against the controller that the refusal to hand over the video recording had violated the GDPR.
While the remedies under Articles 77–79 GDPR may be pursued concurrently and independently of one another, the court pointed out that the coordination of administrative and civil court decisions is a matter for national law in accordance with the principle of procedural autonomy of the Member States. The court held that the requirement of a substantive adverse effect is an appropriate means of avoiding conflicting decisions on the same data protection matter in light of the principle of effectiveness. According to the court, such a requirement helps ensure the uniform application of data protection law and increases legal certainty.

title: VG Berlin - 42 K 72/25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The controller, a fire brigade, employed the data subject who worked in an administrative role in the back office and was not assigned to provide direct assistance to vulnerable persons.
In connection with the COVID-19 pandemic, the controller informed the State Office for Health and Social Affairs (LAGeSo) that the data subject had not provided proof of vaccination or recovery, or a medical certificate confirming a contraindication to COVID-19 vaccination, by the statutory deadline of 15 March 2022. In the notification form, the controller also indicated that the data subject had direct contact with members of vulnerable groups.
The data subject disputed this information and complained to the DPA. He also requested information about the data transmitted to LAGeSo, including a copy of the completed form.
The controller explained that it had been required to report all employees who had not submitted the necessary vaccination, recovery or medical exemption documents. It considered the reporting obligation applicable to all its employees, regardless of their actual duties. It told the data subject it retained no copy of the form.
In 2022, the DPA informed the data subject that it had found no violation of the GDPR. Following separate court proceedings concerning the DPA's handling of the complaint (case VG 1 K 340/22), the DPA withdrew that decision and reconsidered the matter.
The controller maintained that the data subject had remained fit for emergency service and could have been assigned to emergency rescue work at short notice. It also argued that it had provided the data subject with complete information about the data transmitted.
In 2025, the DPA issued a warning against the controller. The state of Berlin challenged this warning in behalf of the controller.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The court dismissed the action and upheld the DPA's warning under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR. It found that the controller had committed two GDPR violations.
First, the controller had violated the accuracy principle under Article 5(1)(d) GDPR.
The court considered that the information in the notification form concerning the data subject's direct contact with vulnerable groups constituted personal data under Article 4(1) GDPR. By transmitting this information, the controller had processed personal data within the meaning of Article 4(2) GDPR and acted as the controller under Article 4(7) GDPR.
The court found that the information was inaccurate. At the time of the notification, the data subject worked exclusively in the back office and had no direct contact with vulnerable persons. The fact that he might have had contact with colleagues working in emergency rescue services did not establish direct contact with vulnerable patients. The controller therefore must assess each employee's actual circumstances individually rather than automatically answer the question in the affirmative for all employees.
Second, the controller had violated Articles 15 and 12(1) GDPR by failing to provide complete access to the data subject's personal data. Although the controller had initially provided some information, its response did not reproduce all the personal data contained in the notification form and some of that subsequent information did not accurately reflect the answers recorded in the form.
The controller's later offer to provide a copy of the form did not remedy the violation. The one-month period for responding to an access request under Article 12(3) GDPR had already expired.
Third, the court found that the DPA had properly exercised its discretion when issuing the warning. It also considered the warning proportionate. A warning under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR was the mildest corrective measure expressly provided for by the GDPR. The fact that the events had occurred more than three years earlier and that the relevant COVID-19 reporting obligation had since ceased to apply did not make the warning disproportionate. 
German law provided for limitation periods for administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, through § 41(2) BDSG in conjunction with the German Administrative Offences Act (OWiG). However, it contained no equivalent provision for corrective measures under Article 58(2) GDPR. The court therefore rejected the application of those limitation rules, including by analogy, to the warning.
Consequently, the court upheld the warning and dismissed the action.

title: VG Berlin - 42 K 66/25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject worked for the controller, a fire brigade, in the back office.
The controller submitted a notification to the State Office for Health and Social Affairs (LAGeSo) concerning the data subject's failure to provide proof of vaccination, recovery from COVID-19 or a medical exemption. It included information that he had direct contact with members of vulnerable groups, which was incorrect (for more details on this matter of the case, see related case 42 K 72/25 between the same parties).
The controller initiated disciplinary proceedings against the data subject, which were later discontinued.
The data subject requested €5,000 in compensation for immaterial damages, arguing that the disclosure of inaccurate information and the allegedly incomplete response to his access request in connection to the disciplinary proceedings and possible sanctions had caused him anxiety, stress and health problems as well as contributed to the ending of his romantic relationship. The controller rejected the request. 
It argued that the disclosure was legally required and maintained that the information in the notification was accurate because the data subject could be deployed in emergency medical services with vulnerable groups. Finally, it disputed that the alleged GDPR infringements had caused the data subject any damage.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The court partially upheld the claim and ordered the controller to pay the data subject €100 in compensation under Article 82(1) GDPR. It dismissed the remainder of the claim.
First, the court held that the controller had infringed the principle of accuracy under Article 5(1)(d) GDPR by stating in the notification to LAGeSo that the data subject had direct contact with members of vulnerable groups, when that was false. It considered the disclosure, apart from the inaccurate information, lawful under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR in conjunction with Article 6(3) GDPR.
Second, the court held that the inaccurate information caused the data subject immaterial damages within the meaning of Article 82(1) GDPR. However, it considered that the information had been disclosed to a limited and identifiable group of recipients, and he had also received a copy of the notification, allowing him to clarify his professional activities and exercise his rights to rectification and erasure under Articles 16 and 17 GDPR. Furthermore, the inaccurate information did not constitute special category personal data under Article 9(1) GDPR.
The court was not convinced that the data subject had suffered additional psychological harm as a result of the inaccurate information, as there was insufficient evidence that his reported anxiety, stress and illness had resulted from the inaccurate statement rather than from the disciplinary proceedings. It emphasised that compensation under Article 82 GDPR served a compensatory, not a punitive or deterrent, purpose. Consequently, the amount of compensation had to reflect the actual damage suffered. 
It rejected any additional compensation based on the controller's duty of care under civil service law.

title: BVwG - W254 2342303-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data controller, a firm involved in the glass and glazing industry, uploaded personal files and information of its data subjects on an unprotected and publicly accessible website. XXXX had stored invoices from at least 75 customers, which contained specific personal data, including first and last names, addresses, customer numbers, and ordered articles, on a unprotected web server, thereby allowing the invoices to be indexed by the Google search engine. This information and data was thus directly accessible with a simple Google search query. Crucially, the accessible information included a directly accessible Excel spreadsheet with  first and last names and email addresses of approximately 580 customers.
The Data Protection Authority assessed and initially fined XXXX, based on a complaint from a data subject and former customer of the controller. This was a result of a erasure request of thee data subject, where the controller relied on Google as a relevant contact and authority for data storage and erasure.
The Data Protection Authority fined the controller an initial fine of 16,800€ with additional litigation costs of 1,680€ amounting to a total fine of 18,480€. 
The Data Protection Authority reasoned that the violation of the principles of integrity and confidentiality within the meaning of Art. 5(1)(f) of the GDPR and the lack of legitimate grounds under Art. 6 GDPR, by the controller, with the lack protection of the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and storage limitation under Art. 5(1(a,b,e)) GDPR, resulted in the steep amount of the issued fine. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Court held that the violations by the controller and their determination by the DPA are largely correct. The Court confirmed that the controller is responsible for the relevant IP address where the exposed personal data of the data subjects could be accessed, the controller did not investigate, analyse or resolve the alleged data breach and that the controller acted negligently relating to the faulty server structure. It confirmed further that the controller failed to grant a minimum level of care and attention to the server structure of the website, to comply with the minimum data protection requirements within the meaning of Articles 5 and 6 of the GDPR. Lastly, the Court highlighted that the controller further refused to implement any corrective measures when notified of the faulty server structure by the data subject, fulfilling the requirements for determining the presence of conditional intent resulting in a larger data protection breach.
Nevertheless, the core of the Court's decision focused on the fine determination and assessment made by the DPA. The Court took into account EDPB's Guidelines on calculation of administrative fines, where the Court emphasised the assessment consists of three elements. These include: the classification of infringements under Art. 83(4-6) GDPR, the gravity of the infringement, and the enterprise’s turnover as a relevant factor to be taken into account when imposing an effective, deterrent, and proportionate administrative fine pursuant to Art. 83(1) GDPR.
Applying it to the present case, the Court highlighted that in determining the fine, the authority should take into account the controller's sensitivity to administrative fines, where the information on the controller's revenue is not available. Stressing this, the Court pointed to the required effect of the fines, where the larger the enterprise, the lower its sensitivity to penalties generally is, and the higher the fine must typically be set so that it can have its specific corrective and preventive effect. 
In this instance, the Court found that the authority's decision to increase the level of the fine from the base amount 0.4% of the total revenue to 0.56%, was not substantiated in detail. In this aspect, the Court stated that the authority, by increasing the fine percentage, without appropriate justifications, is to be regarded as an abuse of discretion. Since, the authority failed to provide comprehensible justification for the discretion in the fine determination, such a determination was found to be incorrect. 
Therefore, the Court, taking the above considerations into account, accordingly adjusted the initial fine, to the proportionate level of an administrative fine of 12,000€, considering the underlying violations and the circumstances. The complaint was therefore granted to this extent, and the administrative fine was reduced to 12,000€.

title: Datatilsynet (Denmark) - 2026-423-0075
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA initiated an investigation on the use of AI-based monitoring systems by the Municipality of Faabord-Midtfyn’s (the controllers) in a nursing home. This system was acquired and put into operation by the controller for a limited six-month trial period on 18 residents of the home. It operated on the basis of AI and camera-based technologies which analyse movement patterns. The intention and purpose behind the implementation of the system was to increase the resident’s sense of security, prevent falls, and support professional assessments of the staff.
In its defence, the controller claimed that it had conducted a risk assessment regarding the use of this system. The risk assessment indicated that the AI-system was not considered essential nor critical and identified potential threats. Ultimately, the controller assessed the impact and likelihood of the identified threats and classified them all as low-risk. As a result of this classification, the controller did not deem it necessary to implement any mitigating measures and neither to conduct a data protection impact assessment. Finally, the controller further clarified that it relied on Article 6(1)(e) and Article 9(2)(g) GDPR as the legal basis to process personal and sensitive data. The controller further expressed its reliance on the national Social Services to justify the reason for this AI systems use.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the risk assessment conducted by the controller was inadequate. Particularly because the assessment did not adequately identify and address the most significant risks posed by the AI system on the residents of the nursing home. Rather the assessment provided for general threats and those posing a low risk. In addition to this, the controller was unable to justification that the identified threats constitute a low risk. Therefore, the DPA held that the controller did not provide for a level of security proportional to the risks posed by the system and associated processing operations.
In addition to this, the DPA stated that the controller should have conducted an adequate data protection impact assessment before putting the system into use at the nursing home. The DPA emphasised the use of a new technology which processes sensitive personal data of vulnerable individuals. In that regard, the six-month trial period did not alleviate the controller from its GDPR obligations.
Finally, the DPA held that the national law legal basis relied upon by the controller was not sufficient for the use of the AI system. The DPA addressed the referred to rules on safety-enhancing welfare technology which allow for the use of systems such as AI, under certain conditions. Nonetheless, the DPA held that the controller did not sufficiently take these rules, which establish a framework for the use of safety-enhancing welfare technology, into account when discussing legal basis of processing.
In light of the foregoing, the DPA reprimanded the controller for conducting processing operations in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and (2), 24(1), 32(1) and 35(1) GDPR. The DPA emphasised that if the controller plans to use the AI system, proper consideration must be taken regarding whether the processing undertaken by the system requires a data protection impact assessment and risk assessment.

title: CJEU - C-654/25 - Undelam
text:
Contents

1 English Summary

1.1 Facts
1.2 Advocate General Opinion

1.2.1 1. Question: identifiability of the data subject
1.2.2 2. Question: Immaterial damages
1.2.3 3. Question: Abuse of rights under Union law
1.2.4 4. Conclusion:


1.3 Holding





English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A provider of a website (controller) used Google Fonts on its website. Google Fonts enables the use of different fonts on the website free of charge. By default, the fonts are loaded from a Google server, which results in the automated transfer of dynamic IP addresses of the user of the website to the US. The controller did not make use of a setting that disallows the data transfer.
Through an automated system that detected the implementation of Google Fonts on a website and automatically accesses the website in order to trigger the transfer of the dynamic IP address to the US, a data subject’s IP address was transferred to the US after a visit on the controller’s website. The data subject then requested the controller to pay a monetary compensation for the data transfer as a settlement, which the controller paid. When the controller found out that the data subject has used this method on thousands of website providers, they reclaimed the money.
The Regional Court of Hannover (Amtsgericht Hannover) ruled that the data subject shall partly repay the controller. Upon appeal, the Higher Regional Court of Hannover (Landgericht Hannover) ruled that the data subject shall repay the full amount, on the basis that they made the claim in abuse of rights. The data subject appealed that decision to the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof). According to the Federal Court of Justice, the controller’s claim depended on the question whether the data subject has suffered immaterial damages pursuant to Article 82 GDPR. Therefore, the Federal Court of Justice referred the question to the CJEU whether a dynamic IP address can be considered personal data, regarding the question of identifiability in particular. With the second question, the referring court asks for the interpretation of “immaterial damages” in case the data subject intentionally provoked the infringement. Lastly, the referring court asks for the prerequisites of an abuse of rights under Union Law when the circumstances of the claim are provoked by the claimant for the purpose of a financial advantage.


Advocate General Opinion[edit | edit source]
1. Question: identifiability of the data subject[edit | edit source]
According to Advocate General Szpunar (AG), data is personal data pursuant to Article 4(1) GDPR when the entity that processes the data can identify the data subject by combining the personal data in question with other data, using the means accessible to them or to third persons. The question of identifiability is to be assessed not from an objective perspective, but from the perspective of the entity that has access to the data (subjective approach). The abstract possibility that someone is capable of identifying the data subject is not sufficient. 
Data is personal data for an entity when the entity, or third parties that are recipients of the data, have the means to likely identify the data subject, having access to additional means that enable identification. In that case, the data is personal data for the third party who possesses all the information to identify the data subject (recipient), as well as indirectly, for the sender.
For the case at hand, this means that when the recipient of the automatically collected dynamic IP address has the means that likely enable the identification of the data subject, the dynamic IP address is personal data for the recipient as well as for the sender. The question whether the sender can identify the data subject, and therefore the question whether the data is personal data for that entity, is irrelevant. The relevant question is whether the recipient of the IP addresses has the means to likely identify the data subject. In case of the affirmative, the data is also personal data for the sender.
As far as the means are concerned that are likely used to identify the data subject, all objective factors such as cost and required amount of time for identification as well as the available technology at that time are to be considered. Therefore, according to the AG, the determining factor to assess whether there are means that can likely identify the data subject, is whether there is a risk of identification. In line with the CJEU’s interpretation of a wide scope of personal data, the threshold for assuming a risk of identification must be low. It is not necessary that the possibility of identification can be proven, but that there is a considerable risk of identification. 
Google possesses an extensive amount of personal data that could enable Google, by combining data, to draw conclusions about the private life of the data subject. This is because the purpose of the data transfer in this case is to personalise the service according to the user’s habits and preferences. It is for the referring court to decide whether the combination of the IP address and other data that Google has access to, enables to draw conclusions on the user’s private life. In this case, there is a considerable risk of identification. Consequently, the dynamic IP address is to be considered personal data for the sender, and the sender acts as controller. 
In order to avoid the situation that the sender is to be considered controller and thus has to oblige the GDPR because of a circumstance that is outside their sphere of influence (the likely identification by the recipient), the AG added another criterium for determining identifiability on the subjective side: the sender must know or should have known that the recipient possesses the means to likely identify the data subject.

2. Question: Immaterial damages[edit | edit source]
According to the AG, the notion of “material or immaterial damage” pursuant to Article 82 GDPR is a notion of Union law, not national law, and must therefore to be interpreted uniformly within the Union. 
The mere fact that the controller violated a provision of the GDPR does not allow the conclusion that the data subject suffered a damage. In reference to CJEU case law, it is not necessary that the data has been used improperly. If suffices when the data subject has suffered a loss of control over their personal data, or that the data subject reasonably fears a loss of control.  
The AG opined that in the case at hand, the data subject has not lost control of their personal data because the data has been processed exactly in the way intended by the data subject. This is because the data subject provoked the data transfer to Google. The data subject did not fear an improper use of their data, they accepted the risk thereof by using the software that automatically accesses websites that use Google Fonts. 

3. Question: Abuse of rights under Union law[edit | edit source]
An abuse of rights presupposes subjective and objective circumstances. On the objective side, the goal of the respective provision must be missed despite the fact that all conditions of the provision are fulfilled. On the subjective side, the person must have the intention of receiving a legal benefit by intentionally creating the circumstances that lead to the fulfilment of the provision.  
Because the data subject automatically accessed thousands of websites and therefore provoked the damage, and accepted a financial advantage in return of not further pursuing their rights, the AG concludes that the data subject acted with the intention of arbitrary creating the applicability of the GDPR. The data subject’s claim that they intended to make the website providers aware of the data privacy problem did not change that opinion. According to the AG, the main goal of the data subject was to pursue a financial advantage. 

4. Conclusion:[edit | edit source]
According to the AG, data is personal data for the sender when the recipient has the means to likely identify the data subject. In case the recipient can combine the data in question with other data, and is capable of drawing conclusions about the private life of the data subject, and the sender knows or should have known about these circumstances, the data is personal data for the sender.
The data subject did not suffer an immaterial damage because he did not suffer a loss of control over their data. This is because they provoked the improper use of their data.
The data subject intentionally created the circumstances that led to the violation of the GDPR in order to benefit financially from a violation of the GDPR. This is an abuse of rights, according to the AG.

Holding[edit | edit source]
tbd
